194 FERC ¶ 61,214
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ON COMPLAINT

(Issued March 19, 2026)

On January 5, 2026, Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company (SIGE) filed a complaint (Complaint) pursuant to sections 202(c), 306, and 309 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) and Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, proposing revisions to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (Tariff) to add a provision (Proposed Tariff Provision) to allocate the costs of keeping Unit 2 of the F.B. Culley generating plant (Culley Unit 2) in operation, in response to the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) December 23, 2025 Emergency Order No. 202-25-13 (DOE Order), under section 202(c) of the FPA and section 301 of the DOE Organization Act.  
In this order, we grant the Complaint and find that the Proposed Tariff Provision is just and reasonable, subject to the outcome of the proceeding in Docket No. ER25-3425.  We direct MISO to make a compliance filing, within 30 days of the date of a Commission order accepting MISO’s compliance filing in Docket No. ER25-3425, to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision, as revised, as discussed below.
Background
Culley Unit 2 Retirement Plan
Culley Unit 2, located in southwestern Indiana, is a coal-fired unit that has a nameplate capacity of 103.7 MW.  Culley Unit 2 is owned and operated by SIGE, a utility operating subsidiary of CenterPoint Energy, Inc.  SIGE planned to retire the unit on December 31, 2025, pursuant to commitments SIGE made in a settlement agreement approved by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (Indiana Commission) in 2025.  SIGE submitted a notice to suspend operation of Culley Unit 2 to MISO pursuant to Attachment Y of the Tariff, and MISO found no reliability violations.
DOE Order
In the DOE Order, the Secretary of Energy determined that “an emergency     exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric energy, a shortage of facilities for the generation of electric energy, and other causes.”  Further, the Secretary of Energy determined that issuance of the DOE Order will “meet the emergency and serve the public interest.”  Therefore, the Secretary of Energy directed MISO and SIGE to take all measures necessary to ensure that Culley Unit 2       is available to operate and directed SIGE to keep Culley Unit 2 open for 90 days, i.e., until March 23, 2026.
The DOE Order cited a statement in the 2024 North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Long-Term Reliability Assessment (Reliability Assessment) that MISO is at risk because “probabilistic assessments indicate above-normal generator outages during extreme weather can result in unserved energy or load loss.  With uncertainty around new resource additions and existing generator retirements, MISO       is also at risk of falling below [Reference Margin Levels] within the next five years.”  The DOE Order quoted a MISO April 2025 presentation on the Planning Resource Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-2026 as demonstrating that, for the MISO    North and MISO Central regions, which include Indiana, “new capacity additions       were insufficient to offset the negative impacts of decreased accreditation, suspensions/retirements and external resources[.]”  The DOE Order also referenced     an annual survey conducted by the Organization of MISO States, Inc. (OMS) and MISO projecting that additional capacity is needed beyond current commitments to meet the projected summer 2026 Planning Reserve Margin and projecting that there would be shortfalls in capacity to meet the peak demand for electricity in each of the following four summers and winters.  The DOE Order noted that the OMS-MISO survey attributed these projected deficits to large quantities of existing generation capacity retirements    and projected accelerated growth of electric demand that would outpace the increase in generation capacity.  The DOE Order noted that MISO’s efforts to address its projected deficiencies to date, particularly through its Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) process, would not immediately add new capacity due to commercial operation dates for ERAS resources that were at least three years away and supply chain constraints that would impede the construction of new capacity.
The DOE Order directed SIGE to “file with [this Commission] Tariff revisions or waivers [necessary] to effectuate [the DOE Order].”
Several entities filed requests for rehearing of the DOE Order with DOE.
SIGE’s Complaint  
SIGE states that it and MISO agree that the Tariff does not have a mechanism     for SIGE to recover costs incurred under the DOE Order.  SIGE therefore asks the Commission to exercise its authority under FPA sections 202(c), 306, and 309 to        order MISO to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision as a cost recovery and allocation mechanism.  SIGE also states that the Proposed Tariff Provision is strictly to establish     a cost allocation mechanism, and that, after the 90-day period (Order Duration Period), SIGE will submit a filing in a separate docket with the actual costs to be allocated according to the Tariff mechanism.  Specifically, SIGE states that it will submit a subsequent filing to the Commission under section 202(c) in which SIGE will explain and support its just and reasonable costs associated with operating Culley Unit 2 and complying with the DOE Order, net of market revenues.
SIGE asserts that the Proposed Tariff Provision meets the “just and reasonable” standard of section 202(c)(1).  In support, SIGE states that section 202(c) requires costs to be allocated based on the scope and nature of the emergency and that the DOE Order referred to the MISO North and MISO Central regions; accordingly, SIGE argues that allocating SIGE’s costs of complying with the DOE Order to both the MISO North and MISO Central regions comports with section 202(c)’s just and reasonable standard.  SIGE notes that the Proposed Tariff Provision is similar to the Tariff provision approved by the Commission with regard to the Consumers Energy Company (Consumers) J.H. Campbell plant (Campbell Plant), and the geographic scope identified in the DOE Order is virtually identical to the scope identified in the DOE emergency order on the Campbell Plant (Campbell Plant DOE Order). 
The Proposed Tariff Provision specifies that it is pursuant to the DOE Order      and applies to the allocation of costs (DOE Order Costs) associated with the continued availability of Culley Unit 2 pursuant to the DOE Order and any extensions ordered by the Secretary of Energy.  The Proposed Tariff Provision states that SIGE will petition the Commission to approve recovery of DOE Order Costs, net of market revenues, and that the costs will be allocated among Local Resource Zones 1-7, i.e., among zones in the MISO North and MISO Central regions, to load-serving entities (LSE) on a “load ratio share” basis.  SIGE notes that the issue of cost allocation on a demand or energy basis is currently pending before the Commission in Docket No. ER25-3425 and that SIGE intends to defer to the Commission’s final decision in that proceeding. 
SIGE argues that the Commission’s prior notice requirements, filed rate     doctrine, and rule against retroactive ratemaking apply to filings or proceedings under sections 205 and 206 of the FPA, but do not apply to determinations and cost recovery under section 202(c).  SIGE argues that section 202(c) allows costs to be determined and recovered after the emergency generation or provision of jurisdictional service.  SIGE maintains that section 202(c)’s contemplation of such post-hoc determinations and recovery is demonstrated in the wording of the statute, including that, after an emergency order “takes effect,” there will be “supplemental” orders regarding “compensation or reimbursement.”  Alternatively, SIGE requests that, if the Commission determines that a section 206 proceeding is necessary, including a finding that the Tariff is unjust and unreasonable and a subsequent determination as to a just and reasonable rate, then the Proposed Tariff Provision should be made effective as of the date of filing of the Complaint. 
Notice and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of the Complaint was published in the Federal Register, 91 Fed. Reg. 994 (Jan. 9, 2026), with interventions and protests due on or before January 26, 2026.
Notices of intervention were filed by:  the Arkansas Public Service Commission (Arkansas Commission); the Council of the City of New Orleans (New Orleans Council); the Illinois Commerce Commission (Illinois Commission); the Louisiana Public Service Commission; the Michigan Public Service Commission; the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission; the Mississippi Public Service Commission; the Missouri Public Service Commission (Missouri Commission); OMS; and the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin.
Timely motions to intervene were filed by:  Alliant Energy Corporate Services, Inc. on behalf of Interstate Power and Light Company and Wisconsin Power and Light Company; Ameren Services Company (Ameren), on behalf of Ameren Illinois Company (Ameren Illinois) and Union Electric Company d/b/a Ameren Missouri; American Electric Power Service Corporation, on behalf of AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Energy Partners, Inc., and AEP Retail Energy Partners LLC; American Municipal Power, Inc.; Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana, Inc. (Citizens Action Coalition); Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin; Consumers; Cooperative Energy; Entergy Services, LLC, on behalf of Entergy Arkansas, LLC, Entergy Louisiana, LLC, Entergy Mississippi, LLC, Entergy New Orleans, LLC, and Entergy Texas, Inc. (collectively, Entergy); Illinois Citizens Utility Board; Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor; the Michigan Attorney General; MISO Transmission Owners;  the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (Illinois Attorney General); Public Citizen, Inc. (Public Citizen); Sierra Club; and Wolverine.  Motions to intervene out of time were filed by Wabash and Environmental Law and Policy Center (ELPC).
On January 26, 2026, MISO submitted its answer to the Complaint.  Protests or comments were filed by:  the Arkansas Commission and the New Orleans Council (collectively, Southern Regulators); the Illinois Attorney General; the Illinois Commission; the Michigan Attorney General; the Missouri Commission; OMS; and Public Interest Organizations.  On February 10, 2026, SIGE filed an answer (SIGE Answer).  On February 11, 2026, Consumers filed an answer (Consumers Answer).
MISO Answer
MISO agrees with SIGE that the Tariff does not currently contain a mechanism  for cost allocation under these circumstances.  MISO states that it does not oppose     the Proposed Tariff Provision and that it will file such a schedule if directed by the Commission.  MISO notes that it reserves the right to change the cost allocation mechanism “to account for existing Tariff requirements and to include other clarifications as may be appropriate.”
Comments and Protests
The Michigan Attorney General and the Illinois Commission state that, contrary  to claims made by the DOE Order, there is no evidence of an energy emergency.  The Illinois Commission asserts that MISO does not need the capacity provided by Culley Unit 2 and that MISO has emergency operating procedures, which both belie the notion of an emergency in MISO.  The Illinois Commission further states that the DOE Order is an overreach of federal authority because it encroaches on that state’s role in resource adequacy and fuel choice.
The Michigan Attorney General opposes the Proposed Tariff Provision, arguing that the Commission should reject it because the underlying DOE Order justifying       cost recovery is ultra vires, and, absent a valid legal obligation to operate pursuant         to FPA section 202(c), the imposition of the costs of operating Culley Unit 2 on ratepayers pursuant to FPA sections 205 or 206 is not just and reasonable and is unduly discriminatory or preferential, and violates the filed rate doctrine.  Alternatively, the Michigan Attorney General requests that the Commission, under the discretion afforded the Commission under FPA section 202(c), issue an order deferring any finding, on the basis that the Proposed Tariff Provision is premature until the rehearing requests at DOE are resolved.  The Michigan Attorney General also asserts that the Commission should limit cost recovery to those costs from the limited scope of operation ordered by the DOE Order if the Commission accepts the Proposed Tariff Provision.  The Michigan Attorney General also notes that the DOE Order requires that MISO “take every step to employ economic dispatch” of Culley Unit 2 in order “to minimize cost to ratepayers” and argues that any form of commitment and dispatch that enables Culley Unit 2 to operate at a net loss in its market operations, factoring the costs of repairs necessary to be operable, is inconsistent with the DOE Order.  The Michigan Attorney General states that the Commission should impose a “clawback” mechanism to refund upgrade costs recovered under the Proposed Tariff Provision should Culley Unit 2 return to commercial operation and require provisions for refunds of unlawful charges to customers in the event the DOE Order is invalidated.
In addition, the Michigan Attorney General argues that costs should be recovered throughout the entire MISO region to be consistent with cost causation principles.  The Michigan Attorney General explains that the DOE Order asserts that there is an emergency throughout the entire MISO region and that its assessment of an emergency is not limited to specific zones in MISO.  The Michigan Attorney General also notes that if the DOE Order is valid then operating Culley Unit 2 would be needed to comply with federal law, and Commission precedent has allocated the costs of complying with a law across the law’s applicable jurisdiction, in this case the entire MISO region.
Public Interest Organizations state that the Commission should reject the Complaint because ratepayers should not be subject to costs for unlawful section 202(c) orders, or that the Commission, at a minimum, should delay acting on the Complaint until issues related to the validity and scope of the DOE Order have concluded.  Public Interest Organizations request that if the Commission determines that creating a cost allocation mechanism is appropriate, the Commission should, at a minimum, make clear that any and all costs assigned pursuant to the Proposed Tariff Provision are subject to refund if the underlying DOE Order is found unlawful.  
Public Interest Organizations also argue that the Commission cannot approve any compensation for the capacity contributions of Culley Unit 2 because the DOE Order states that the units will not be considered capacity resources.  Public Interest Organizations add that LSEs in MISO have sufficient capacity such that they will not benefit from additional capacity from Culley Unit 2.  
Further, Public Interest Organizations explain that MISO has existing Tariff provisions to compensate for and allocate the costs of Culley Unit 2’s participation in    the energy and ancillary services market, as the Tariff compensates generators during periods of scarcity through the Value of Lost Load (VOLL) mechanism, which is a     price cap implemented during MISO emergency events.  Given this Tariff mechanism, Public Interest Organizations argue that SIGE must demonstrate that recovery of its    costs are not compensated by existing Tariff provisions.  In addition, Public Interest Organizations argue that SIGE should demonstrate what, if any, uncompensated benefits are provided by the continued operation of Culley Unit 2 and the relative level of benefits each Local Resource Zone receives.  Public Interest Organizations allege that SIGE has not justified the load ratio share concept in the Proposed Tariff Provision, as the benefits of the continued operation of the unit do not appear to align with the average amount of electricity withdrawn by each LSE.
Multiple commenters request that the Commission require MISO to initiate a stakeholder process related to the Proposed Tariff Provision.  The Illinois Attorney General argues that the DOE Order may be extended or other section 202(c) orders may be issued; therefore, a stakeholder process is needed to address how plants will be compensated in these circumstances.  The Illinois Commission states that, after such a stakeholder process, the Commission should set the matter for hearing to develop a record of the costs that have been informed by the results of a stakeholder process.  The Illinois Commission adds that a stakeholder process is necessary because the capacity provided by Culley Unit 2 is not needed in MISO.  Similarly, OMS urges the Commission to direct MISO to engage with MISO states and stakeholders in determining any cost recovery or cost allocation methods.  OMS requests that, absent such direction from the Commission, the Commission should set the Complaint for hearing.  The Missouri Commission avers that stakeholders are entitled to increased transparency regarding the use and costs related to orders issued under section 202(c); consequently, the Missouri Commission states that the Commission should direct SIGE and other plant owners subject to future section 202(c) orders to submit regular reports into these proceedings on their plants’ operation and costs. 
OMS asserts that to satisfy the just and reasonable standard required by law,      any cost allocation method must demonstrate a clear nexus between the costs incurred and the benefits received, and in evaluating whether such a relationship exists, material differences among states and regions must be considered, including variations in load forecasts, resource mix, retirement schedules, and system conditions.  OMS states that routine Commission approval of broad allocation for costs associated with a section 202(c) order may incentivize utilities to accelerate retirements and cash in on a section 202(c) order cost shift, moving costs away from local customers and onto an 11-state region.  OMS argues that relying on arbitrary regional cost allocation may shield utilities from political and economic consequences, distort market signals, and create perverse incentives to prolong emergency operations.
Southern Regulators take no position on SIGE’s requested relief, the Commission’s authority to grant that relief, or whether the Proposed Tariff Provision is just and reasonable, but request that any Commission order on the Complaint make clear that any rate recovery schedule that the Commission may accept in this proceeding      will not be of general applicability under the Tariff but will be limited to Culley Unit 2 and costs incurred due to the DOE Order.  They also assert that costs should not be allocated to the MISO South region, and they urge the Commission to make clear that any findings on cost allocation in this proceeding do not set precedent for future DOE orders issued pursuant to section 202(c). 
	C.	Answers to Comments and Protests
In response to arguments that the Commission should establish a hearing to determine the beneficiaries of the continued operation of Culley Unit 2, SIGE states that the Commission’s acceptance of the Proposed Tariff Provision is not predicated on SIGE demonstrating cost causation or identifying the beneficiaries.  SIGE states that, pursuant to section 202(c), the costs of Culley Unit 2’s continued operation are to be allocated in accordance with the scope of the emergency identified in the DOE Order.  SIGE argues that a hearing is unnecessary because there are no material facts in dispute that would require a hearing.  SIGE also objects to requests for a MISO stakeholder process, arguing that a stakeholder process is unwarranted because it would delay cost recovery and because the DOE Order directed the Commission, and not MISO, to address the cost recovery issue.  SIGE underscores that any DOE Order Costs that it seeks to recover in the future will be the subject of a separate proceeding in which SIGE will identify and support its right to recover specific costs.  SIGE states that all impacted parties will have an opportunity to participate in that proceeding.  At this juncture, SIGE states that it is merely seeking to have an appropriate cost recovery mechanism added to the Tariff consistent with the DOE Order, the FPA, and Commission precedent.
Consumers also objects to the requests for a MISO stakeholder process, arguing that section 202(c) and the DOE Order direct the Commission, not MISO, to address cost recovery issues.  In addition, Consumers argues that concerns with the DOE Order or the Commission’s determinations regarding cost recovery issues are properly addressed through rehearing and judicial review processes, not through a stakeholder process.  Consumers notes that the fact that DOE has issued additional orders under section 202(c) should lead the Commission to follow the process established for the Campbell Plant, rather than impose a new process.  However, Consumers argues in the alternative that, if the Commission does change course and directs MISO to hold a stakeholder process on Culley Unit 2, the Commission should clarify that such a stakeholder process should be prospective-only and would not affect the cost recovery process in place for the Campbell Plant.
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the notices of intervention and the timely, unopposed motions to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding.
Pursuant to Rule 214(d) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,   18 C.F.R. § 385.214(d), we grant the late-filed motions to intervene given Wabash’s and ELPC’s interest in the proceeding, the early stage of the proceeding, and the absence of undue prejudice or delay.
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by SIGE and Consumers because they provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters 
As discussed below, we grant SIGE’s Complaint and find the Proposed Tariff Provision is just and reasonable under FPA section 202(c), subject to the outcome of     the proceeding in Docket No. ER25-3425.  Accordingly, we direct MISO to make a compliance filing to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision.  MISO should file the compliance filing, within 30 days of the date of a Commission order accepting MISO’s compliance filing in Docket No. ER25-3425, to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision, as discussed below.
The DOE Organization Act gives the Secretary of Energy the authority pursuant to section 202(c) of the FPA that had been previously granted to the Federal Power Commission.  Responsibilities pursuant to section 202(c) include taking action to address an energy emergency: 
(c) Temporary connection and exchange of facilities during emergency
(1) . . . [W]henever the Commission determines that an emergency exists by reason of a sudden increase in the demand for electric energy, or a shortage of electric energy or of facilities for the generation or transmission of electric energy, or of fuel or water for generating facilities, or other causes, the Commission shall have authority, either upon its own motion or upon complaint, with or without notice, hearing, or report, to require by order such temporary connections of facilities and such generation, delivery, interchange, or transmission of electric energy as in its judgment will best meet the emergency and serve the public interest. 

Section 202(c)(1) also provides for affected parties to agree on terms, and, if that fails, then, after a hearing, terms may be prescribed as follows:

If the parties affected by such order fail to agree upon the terms of any arrangement between them in carrying out such order, the Commission, after hearing held either before or after such order takes effect, may prescribe by supplemental order such terms as it finds to be just and reasonable, including the compensation or reimbursement which should be paid to or by any such party.

The Commission’s rate analysis applies the cost causation principle, which requires that “all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them.”  We find that this is the relevant legal standard for evaluating whether the proposed method to allocate the costs of keeping Culley Unit 2 in operation, in response to the DOE Order, is just and reasonable.  Courts have explained that, to “the extent that a utility benefits from the costs of new facilities, it may be said to have ‘caused’ a part of those costs to be incurred, as without the expectation of its contributions the facilities might not have been built, or might have been delayed.”      As a result, a cost allocation method can satisfy the cost causation principle if the Commission “has an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits are        at least roughly commensurate with” the allocation of the costs.  
In applying the cost causation principle here, we find that it is just and reasonable for the cost allocation method to allocate costs in accordance with the scope of the emergency as described by the DOE Order.  We recognize that the parties offer different interpretations of the DOE Order on that issue.  SIGE argues that the beneficiaries are the LSEs in Local Resource Zones 1-7, which the DOE Order refers to as MISO North and MISO Central.  Public Interest Organizations challenge SIGE’s interpretation of the DOE Order, noting that LSEs in MISO as a whole and in Indiana specifically have already met their resource adequacy requirements, such that they would not benefit from the extra capacity from Culley Unit 2.  The Michigan Attorney General argues that the DOE Order supports a MISO-wide cost allocation, including to MISO South.
We acknowledge that parties have presented different interpretations of how the DOE Order defined the geographic scope of the emergency.  However, we find that, as with the Campbell Plant DOE Order, the most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued operation of Culley  Unit 2 is in the MISO North and MISO Central regions, i.e., Local Resource Zones 1-7.  Specifically, we find that it is reasonable to interpret the DOE Order’s reliance on statements in MISO’s presentation on the Planning Resource Auction Results for Planning Year 2025-2026 that “new capacity additions were insufficient to offset the negative impacts of decreased accreditation, suspensions/retirements and external resources” in the MISO North and MISO Central regions as indicating that resource adequacy concerns for those regions were the driver for the DOE Order.  Therefore, we accept SIGE’s proposal to allocate the costs of keeping Culley Unit 2 in operation, in response to the DOE Order, to LSEs within Local Resource Zones 1-7.
Public Interest Organizations argue that SIGE must demonstrate the relative    level of benefits each Local Resource Zone receives and that benefits may not accrue      in a way that aligns with the average amount of electricity withdrawn by each LSE in Local Resource Zones 1-7.  However, as the Commission found in the order accepting the cost allocation mechanism precipitated by the Campbell Plant DOE Order, a load ratio share allocation method based on actual peak demand reasonably aligns the allocation of the Campbell Plant DOE Order Costs with the emergency described in      the Campbell Plant DOE Order and the beneficiaries of the continued operation of the Campbell Plant.  We apply similar reasoning to Culley Unit 2, as well.  We also note that the Proposed Tariff Revision will use peak demand to allocate costs among LSEs in Local Resource Zones 1-7, which is consistent with the Commission’s recent order on MISO’s compliance filing in Docket No. ER25-3425.  
In response to commenters who argue that the Commission should require MISO to initiate a stakeholder process related to the Proposed Tariff Provision, we find that further process is not necessary.  As described above, the most reasonable reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued operation of Culley Unit 2 is in Local Resource Zones 1-7, providing sufficient basis for our accepting SIGE’s proposal.  Similarly, we decline to require SIGE to submit regular reports on Culley Unit 2’s continued operation and costs in this proceeding, having found that a stakeholder process is unnecessary and the Proposed Tariff Revision is just and reasonable.  Further, we note that the instant proceeding has provided any interested stakeholder notice of SIGE’s proposal and an opportunity to comment.  We also reject commenters’ request to delay action on the Proposed Tariff Provision until the rehearing proceeding at DOE is resolved, as prompt action on the Complaint can help to mitigate potential regulatory uncertainty.  
We find that arguments related to the prudence of costs associated with operating Culley Unit 2 are beyond the limited scope of this proceeding.  We also find that whether the Proposed Tariff Provision should include a mechanism to refund upgrade costs recovered under the Proposed Tariff Provision should Culley Unit 2 continue to operate beyond the term of the DOE Order is likewise beyond the limited scope of this proceeding.  Public Interest Organizations assert that SIGE must demonstrate what, if any, uncompensated benefits are provided by the continued operation of Culley Unit 2.  They also assert that the recovery of DOE Order Costs is covered by existing Tariff provisions, particularly the Tariff’s VOLL mechanism.  We disagree.  While existing Tariff provisions govern the distribution of market revenues for any energy supplied by Market Participants, they do not provide a cost allocation method for prudently incurred costs associated with orders issued under FPA section 202(c) directing resources to ensure continuing availability for operation, such as the DOE Order Costs.  Under the Proposed Tariff Provision, any market revenue, including any revenue based on scarcity pricing, will be netted from the DOE Order Costs, and recovery of any DOE Order Costs in excess of market revenue is outside the scope of this proceeding.  While this order approves the cost allocation method in the Proposed Tariff Provision, subject to condition, it does not approve recovery of actual costs.  Pursuant to the Proposed Tariff Provision, SIGE must petition the Commission in a separate proceeding at a later date for approval to recover specific DOE Order Costs before ratepayers can be charged for such costs.  Parties may raise issues related to the scope of costs prudently incurred pursuant to the DOE Order in that cost recovery proceeding.  Parties also may take appropriate steps, such as requesting rehearing in this proceeding, to preserve arguments that, if the DOE Order were to be modified, then the Commission should require refunds or otherwise revisit its approach to matters in connection with the DOE Order.
Furthermore, we find that the DOE Order’s statement that Culley Unit 2 “shall not be considered a capacity resource” does not mean that the Commission cannot approve compensation that arises from Culley Unit 2’s capacity benefits.  Regardless of whether Culley Unit 2 is treated as a capacity resource in MISO’s resource adequacy construct, the DOE Order cited resource adequacy concerns for the MISO North and MISO Central regions as the driver of the need for continued operation of Culley Unit 2.
We find OMS’ argument that granting the Complaint may incentivize utilities to accelerate retirements is speculative, as OMS provides no additional explanation of such potential behavior.
Accordingly, we grant SIGE’s Complaint and find the Proposed Tariff Provision is just and reasonable under FPA section 202(c), subject to the outcome of the proceeding in Docket No. ER25-3425.  We direct MISO to make a compliance filing, within 30 days of the date of a Commission order accepting MISO’s compliance filing in Docket No. ER25-3425, to adopt the Proposed Tariff Provision, including any modifications directed in Docket No. ER25-3425.  The effective date of the provision will be the issuance date of the DOE Order, December 23, 2025.
The Commission orders:

(A)	SIGE’s Complaint is hereby granted, as discussed in the body of this order.
(B)	MISO is hereby directed to file a compliance filing, within 30 days             of the date of a Commission order accepting MISO’s compliance filing in Docket         No. ER25-3425, as discussed in the body of this order.
By the Commission.

( S E A L )							



Debbie-Anne A. Reese,
Secretary.
